source_text: Ἢ κυριώτερος ὁ ἐν ἀπορρήτοις παραδιδόμενος λόγος, ὡς ἄρα ὁ τὴν τοῦ χρόνου φύσιν κατασκευάσας Θεὸς, μέτρα αὐτῷ καὶ σημεῖα τὰ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐπέβαλε διαστήματα, καὶ ἑβδομάδι αὐτὸν ἐκμετρῶν, ἀεὶ τὴν ἑβδομάδα εἰς ἑαυτὴν ἀνακυκλοῦσθαι κελεύει, ἐξαριθμοῦσαν τοῦ χρόνου τὴν κίνησιν. Τὴν ἑβδομάδα δὲ πάλιν ἐκπληροῦν τὴν ἡμέραν μίαν, ἑπτάκις αὐτὴν εἰς ἑαυτὴν ἀναστρέφουσαν, τοῦτο δὲ κυκλικόν ἐστι τὸ σχῆμα, ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ἄρχεσθαι, καὶ εἰς ἑαυτὸ καταλήγειν. Ὃ δὴ καὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος ἴδιον, εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀναστρέφειν, καὶ μηδαμοῦ περα τοῦσθαι. Διὰ τοῦτο τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ χρόνου οὐχὶ πρώτην ἡμέραν, ἀλλὰ μίαν ὠνόμασεν· ἵνα καὶ ἐκ τῆς προσηγορίας τὸ συγγενὲς ἔχῃ πρὸς τὸν αἰῶνα. Τοῦ γὰρ μοναχοῦ ἀκοινωνήτου πρὸς ἕτερον ἡ τὸν χαρακτῆρα δεικνύουσα, οἰκείως καὶ προσφυῶς προσηγορεύθη μία. Εἰ δὲ πολλοὺς ἡμῖν αἰῶνας παρίστησιν ἡ Γραφὴ, αἰῶνα αἰῶνος, καὶ αἰῶνας αἰώνων πολλαχοῦ λέγουσα, ἀλλ' οὖν κἀκεῖ οὐχὶ πρῶτος, οὐδὲ δεύτερος, οὐδὲ τρίτος ἡμῖν αἰὼν ἀπηρίθμηται· ὥστε μᾶλλον καταστάσεων ἡμῖν καὶ πραγμάτων ποικίλων διαφορὰς, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ περιγραφὰς καὶ πέρατα καὶ διαδοχὰς αἰώνων ἐκ τούτου δείκνυσθαι. Ἡμέρα γὰρ Κυρίου, φησὶ, μεγάλη καὶ ἐπιφανής. Καὶ πάλιν, Ἵνα τί ὑμῖν ζητεῖν τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ Κυρίου; Καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶ σκότος καὶ οὐ φῶς. Σκότος δὲ, δηλονότι τοῖς ἀξίοις τοῦ σκότους. Ἐπεὶ ἀνέσπερον καὶ ἀδιάδοχον καὶ ἀτελεύτητον τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην οἶδεν ὁ λόγος, ἣν καὶ ὀγδόην ὁ ψαλμῳδὸς προσηγόρευσε, διὰ τὸ ἔξω κεῖσθαι τοῦ ἑβδοματικοῦ τούτου χρόνου. Ὥστε κἂν ἡμέραν εἴπῃς, κἂν αἰῶνα, τὴν αὐτὴν ἐρεῖς ἔννοιαν. Εἴτε οὖν ἡμέρα ἡ κατάστασις ἐκείνη λέγοιτο, μία ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ πολλαί· εἴτε αἰὼν προσαγορεύοιτο, μοναχὸς ἂν εἴη καὶ οὐ πολλοστός. Ἵνα οὖν πρὸς τὴν μέλλουσαν ζωὴν τὴν ἔννοιαν ἀπαγάγῃ, μίαν ὠνόμασε τοῦ αἰῶνος τὴν εἰκόνα, τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῶν ἡμερῶν, τὴν ὁμήλικα τοῦ φωτὸς, τὴν ἁγίαν κυριακὴν, τὴν τῇ ἀναστάσει τοῦ Κυρίου τετιμημένην. Ἐγένετο οὖν ἑσπέρα, φησὶ, καὶ ἐγένετο πρωΐ, ἡμέρα μία. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ οἱ περὶ τῆς ἑσπέρας ἐκείνης λόγοι ὑπὸ τῆς παρούσης ἑσπέρας καταληφθέντες, ἐνταῦθα ἡμῖν τὸν λόγον ὁρίζουσιν. Ὁ δὲ Πατὴρ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ φωτὸς, ὁ τὴν ἡμέραν κοσμήσας τῷ οὐρανίῳ φωτὶ, ὁ τὴν νύκτα φαιδρύνας ταῖς αὐγαῖς τοῦ πυρὸς, ὁ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν εὐτρεπίσας τῷ νοερῷ καὶ ἀπαύστῳ φωτὶ, φωτίσειεν ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τῆς ἀληθείας, καὶ ἀπρόσκοπον ὑμῶν διατηρήσειε τὴν ζωὴν, παρεχόμενος ἡμῖν, ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατεῖν, ἵνα ἐκλάμψητε, ὡς ὁ ἥλιος ἐν τῇ λαμπρότητι τῶν ἁγίων, εἰς καύχημα ἐμοὶ, εἰς ἡμέραν Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. ΟΜΙΛΙΑ γʹ. Περὶ τοῦ στερεώματος. 3.1 Τὰ τῆς πρώτης ἡμέρας ἔργα, μᾶλλον δὲ τὰ τῆς μιᾶς· μὴ γὰρ οὖν ἀφελώμεθα αὐτῆς τὸ ἀξίωμα, ὃ ἐν τῇ φύσει ἔχει, παρὰ τοῦ κτίσαντος καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἐκδοθεῖσα, οὐκ ἐν τῇ πρὸς τὰς ἄλλας συντάξει ἀριθμηθεῖσα· πλὴν ἀλλ' ὅτι τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ γενόμενα χθὲς ἐπελθὼν ὁ λόγος καὶ διελὼν τὴν ἐξήγησιν τοῖς ἀκροωμένοις, τὴν μὲν ἑωθινὴν τροφὴν τῶν ψυχῶν, τὴν δὲ ἑσπερινὴν εὐφροσύνην ποιησάμενος, νῦν ἐπὶ τὰ τῆς δευτέρας θαύματα μεταβαίνει.
thought_title: Why the first day is called 'one' not 'first'
orientation: Basil is expounding the first day of creation and explaining why Scripture calls it 'one day' rather than 'first day'.
pass_a_gloss: Or the more authoritative account handed down in secret, that the God who constructed the nature of time imposed on it measures and signs, the intervals of days, and measuring it by the week, commands the week always to return in a circle upon itself, counting out the movement of time. And the week again fills up one day, turning seven times upon itself, and this is a circular shape, to begin from itself and to end in itself. Which indeed is also proper to the age, to return upon itself and nowhere to come to an end. For this reason he named the head of time not first day but one day; so that from the name also it may have kinship with the age. For the name showing the character of the solitary and unshared with another was fittingly and suitably called one. But if Scripture presents many ages to us, saying age of age and ages of ages in many places, yet even there neither first nor second nor third age has been counted out for us; so that rather differences of conditions and of varied affairs, but not circumscriptions and limits and successions of ages are shown from this. For the day of the Lord, it says, is great and manifest. And again, Why do you seek the day of the Lord? And this is darkness and not light. Darkness, clearly, for those worthy of the darkness. Since the word knows that day to be without evening and without succession and without end, which also the psalmist called the eighth, because it lies outside this sevenfold time. So that whether you say day or age, you will say the same concept. Whether therefore that condition is called day, it is one and not many; whether it is called age, it would be solitary and not multiple. In order therefore to lead the thought toward the life to come, he named one the image of the age, the firstfruits of the days, the same age as the light, the holy Lord's day, the one honored by the resurrection of the Lord. And there was evening, it says, and there was morning, one day. But indeed the words about that evening, overtaken by the present evening, here set the limit of our discourse. May the Father of the true light, who adorned the day with heavenly light, who brightened the night with the rays of fire, who prepared the rest of the age to come with the intellectual and unceasing light, enlighten your hearts in knowledge of the truth, and keep your life without stumbling, granting us to walk becomingly as in the day, so that you may shine as the sun in the brightness of the saints, for a boast to me, for the day of Christ, to whom be the glory and the might for ever and ever. Amen. Homily 3. On the firmament. 3.1 The works of the first day, or rather of the one day; for let us not take away from it the dignity which it has in its nature, having been given out by the creator by itself, not numbered in the arrangement with the others; but nevertheless, the discourse having gone through the things that happened in it yesterday and having distributed the explanation to the hearers, making the morning food of souls and the evening gladness, now moves on to the wonders of the second day.

choices.english: the more authoritative account handed down in secret
choices.why: ἀπορρήτοις means secret or ineffable; the phrase marks this as a deeper, mystical tradition contrasted with the plain reading
Basil's whole point is that 'one' not 'first' indicates kinship with eternity; the numeral must stay literal
The adjective means alone, single, unaccompanied; Basil is explaining why 'one' suits the day's kinship with the age
κυριακή is the standard term for Sunday, the Lord's day, tied to the resurrection; the literal rendering preserves the liturgical reference
The adjective means not causing or suffering offense, blameless; 'without stumbling' keeps the literal sense of not tripping
περιπατεῖν is the standard Pauline metaphor for conduct; εὐσχημόνως means decently, properly

pass_b_english: Or perhaps the more authoritative account is the one handed down in secret: that the God who fashioned the nature of time imposed measures and signs upon it—the intervals of days—and measuring it by the week, he commands the week always to return in a circle upon itself, counting out the movement of time. And the week, in turn, is completed by one day, returning upon itself seven times—and this is a circular shape, to begin from itself and end in itself. This is also the special property of eternity: to return upon itself and never come to an end. For this reason he named the head of time not “first day” but “one day,” so that even from the name it would have kinship with eternity. For the name that displays the character of what is solitary and unshared with another was fittingly and properly called “one.” And if Scripture presents many ages to us, speaking in many places of “age of age” and “ages of ages,” yet even there no first or second or third age has been counted out for us—so that from this we are shown differences of various conditions and affairs, not boundaries and limits and successions of ages. For “the day of the Lord,” it says, “is great and glorious” (Joel 2:11). And again, “Why do you seek the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). Darkness, clearly, for those who deserve the darkness. For the word knows that day to be without evening, without succession, and without end—the day the psalmist also called the eighth, because it lies outside this sevenfold time. So whether you say “day” or “age,” you will mean the same thing. If that condition is called a day, it is one and not many; if it is called an age, it is solitary and not one of many. So to lead our thought toward the life to come, he named the image of eternity “one”—the firstfruits of days, the same age as the light, the holy Lord’s day, honored by the resurrection of the Lord. “And there was evening,” it says, “and there was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). But the words about that evening have been overtaken by the present evening, and here they bring our discourse to a close. May the Father of the true light, who adorned the day with heavenly light, who brightened the night with the rays of fire, who prepared the rest of the coming age with the spiritual and unceasing light, enlighten your hearts in the knowledge of the truth, and keep your life without stumbling, granting us to walk becomingly as in the day, so that you may shine like the sun in the brightness of the saints, for my boast, for the day of Christ—to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

The works of the first day—or rather, of the one day; for let us not take away from it the dignity it has in its nature, given by the Creator as a day in its own right, not numbered in sequence with the others—the things that came to be on it, then, our discourse went through yesterday and divided the explanation among the hearers, making the morning food for souls and the evening gladness. Now it moves on to the wonders of the second day.

last_rejected.ruling: νοερῷ can mean 'spiritual' in patristic Greek; 'spiritual and unceasing light' is within normal semantic range.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ἵνα τί ὑμῖν ζητεῖν τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ Κυρίου; Καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶ σκότος καὶ οὐ φῶς
last_rejected.why: The source quotes Joel 2:11 and then another verse; the second quote matches Amos 5:18, but Basil attributes both to 'it says' without naming Amos. The English adds '(Amos 5:18)' as a citation, but the work brief says Basil follows LXX book names. More critically, the source text does not name Amos; it uses 'φησὶ' after the Joel citation, then 'Καὶ πάλιν' for the second quote. The English correctly identifies the verse but the source does not attribute it to Amos by name.
last_rejected.fix: Remove '(Amos 5:18)' or verify if Basil's text names the prophet; if not, use 'it says' or 'the prophet says'.
last_rejected.ruling: Source has no scripture reference; English adds '(Amos 5:18)' as helpful citation aid. Not in source text, not a mistranslation of meaning.

last_rejected.quote: the same age as the light
last_rejected.why: 'ὁμήλιξ' means 'of the same age, coeval, contemporary'—the day is coeval with light, not 'the same age as the light' which is awkward and potentially misleading about 'age' as aion.
last_rejected.fix: the coeval of light, or contemporary with light
last_rejected.ruling: 'ὁμήλικα' means coeval/same age; 'same age as the light' is within normal range. Awkwardness is preference, not major error.

last_rejected.quote: granting us to walk becomingly as in the day
last_rejected.source_quote: παρεχόμενος ἡμῖν, ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατεῖν
last_rejected.why: The English omits 'ἡμῖν' (to us/for us), making 'granting us' appear to cover it, but the Greek has 'παρεχόμενος ἡμῖν' (providing to us) as a separate participial clause before 'ἵνα ἐκλάμψητε'. The English merges this awkwardly.
last_rejected.fix: providing for us that we may walk becomingly as in the day
last_rejected.ruling: 'granting us' translates 'παρεχόμενος ἡμῖν'; 'us' renders ἡμῖν. No omission; meaning fully preserved.
